question: Aluminium reacts with air more readily than iron does. Why doesn't a can crumble away the way a nail rusts?
answer: Its oxide stays put. The film on aluminium takes up only a little more room than the metal it replaced, so it clings, a few nanometres thick, and seals the surface. Rust needs about twice the space of its iron, so it cracks and flakes, and each flake bares fresh metal to the air.
move: How readily something reacts matters less than whether its first damage protects it.
source: Pilling and Bedworth, J. Inst. Metals, 1923
reference: Pilling and Bedworth, The oxidation of metals at high temperatures, Journal of the Institute of Metals 29, 529, 1923
